clues.label: IDENTIFY THE COUPLE & THE MOVIE
clues.prompt: This rumored love story became unforgettable because cinema and gossip seemed to look directly at each other. Two actors who had already created huge screen chemistry were cast in a film about a married man, his wife, and the woman he cannot emotionally escape. The casting itself became the real headline, because audiences felt the film was not hiding from the rumors around them — it was almost staging them.

clues.label: IDENTIFY THE COUPLE
clues.prompt: On a legendary film set, the story was supposed to be about a mother and her sons, but off-screen, another love story quietly began. During a fire sequence, the actress was trapped, and a younger co-star rushed in to save her, getting badly burned himself. What began as gratitude slowly became affection, and soon the man playing her son on-screen became her husband in real life.

clues.label: ID THE MOVIE AND THE LEGAL REFERENCE
clues.prompt: In a 2013 Indian Hindi-language thriller, a game with life-altering consequences is central to the plot. Directed by Aditya Datt and produced by Eros International, this film stars Paresh Rawal, Rajeev Khandelwal, and Tina Desai. The storyline delves into the severe implications of ragging, a pressing social issue. Interestingly, the film’s title holds a significant legal reference as well.
clues.answer: Table No. 21 (Ragging is against Article 21 of the Indian Constitution)

clues.label: WHICH SLOGAN IS THIS? WHICH SOFT DRINK?
clues.prompt:
This soft drink brand had plenty of memorable advertising campaigns in India, ever since its entry into the market in the late 1980s.
However probably the best of them lies in the memory of a martyred braveheart, who made the ad slogan his own during the 1999 Kargil War, keeping it alive in public memory, long after the brand had moved to using other jingles. 
It also inspired the title of a 2004 Anant Mahadevan film.

clues.label: NAME THE VOCALIST AND THE FILM
clues.prompt:
A great classical vocalist did not want to sing for films. So when a legendary filmmaker insisted, the vocalist quoted an absurdly high fee (₹25,000 per song for the 1960 when Lata or Rafi charged around ₹300 or ₹400), probably thinking, “Now they will leave me alone.”
Unfortunately for him, the filmmaker was making the cinematic equivalent of a Mughal monument and simply said yes.
The result: the vocalist sang only two film songs in his playback career, both for the same historical epic.

answerImages.source: Mughal-E-Azam (1960) - IMDb
